charts.editorial_rationale: WTI crossed above $100/bbl for the first time since July 2022 this week, a 50%+ monthly gain driven entirely by the Strait of Hormuz closure. The area-threshold chart shows the price line blowing through the $70 conventional breakeven floor — the spatial contrast between where WTI was in early March and where it ended is the central fact of this briefing.
charts.callout_text: WTI crude settled at US$102.88/bbl on March 30 — the first close above $100 since July 2022. The Strait of Hormuz disruption (~20% of global seaborne oil flows) drove a 50%+ monthly advance. The database tracks 42 oil and gas projects ($93.8B) and 317 power and energy projects ($487B) with commodity price linkages across Canada.

charts.editorial_rationale: The loonie fell 1.85% in March despite a 50% WTI surge — the paradox is editorially significant. Normally a petrocurrency like CAD strengthens when oil spikes; this week it weakened, reflecting the 125–150bp rate differential with the Fed and risk-off US dollar demand. The gradient area chart showing CAD/USD month-over-month decline makes the disconnect from oil prices visible.
charts.callout_text: CAD/USD fell to 0.7198 on March 30, down 1.85% month-over-month, as the 125–150 basis point spread between the Bank of Canada's 2.25% policy rate and the Federal Reserve's 3.50–3.75% target weighed on the loonie. The database tracks 653 projects in trade-exposed sectors where FX movements affect input costs or export revenue.

charts.editorial_rationale: The February employment report showed 84,000 net job losses — full-time down 108,000, part-time up 24,000, private sector down 73,000, public sector up 14,000. A diverging bar chart showing the decomposition of the employment change makes the composition of the decline legible in a way the prose cannot. This is the second-largest story of the week behind WTI.
charts.callout_text: Employment declined 84,000 in February 2026, reversing Q4 2025 gains. Full-time positions fell 108,000 while part-time rose 24,000. Private sector shed 73,000 positions and public sector added 14,000. The unemployment rate rose 0.2pp to 6.7%. The database tracks 1,034 projects under construction that depend on labour market conditions.
